answer.text: The Korean War was triggered by the invasion of South Korea by North Korean forces on June 25, 1950.
North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel during the invasion of South Korea on June 25, 1950.
The North Korean People's Army (NKPA) carried out the invasion of South Korea on June 25, 1950.
The North Korean invasion began with troops crossing the 38th parallel into South Korea.
The North Korean attack on June 25, 1950, was a surprise invasion that quickly captured Seoul, the capital of South Korea.
The United States intervened in the Korean War to prevent the spread of communism, aligning with the Cold War strategy of containment.
The Korean War was the first major military conflict of the Cold War and served as a test of the containment doctrine.

General Douglas MacArthur proposed expanding the war into China and using nuclear weapons, prompting internal debates about containing communism versus risking a global conflict, ultimately leading to the war being confined to the Korean Peninsula.
The U.S. believed that if South Korea fell, communist leaders would be emboldened to threaten other nations closer to the West, reinforcing the rationale for intervention.
The United States intervened in the Korean War to prevent the spread of communism, aligning with the Cold War policy of containment.
The North Korean invasion of South Korea on June 25, 1950, directly triggered U.S. military involvement.
The United States committed troops to defend South Korea following the North Korean invasion, with President Truman authorizing General Douglas MacArthur to provide air and naval support.
The Korean War led to a significant increase in military spending, contributing to the development of a powerful military-industrial complex.
The dismissal of General Douglas MacArthur by President Truman triggered a political firestorm and significantly damaged Truman's approval ratings, contributing to the end of his presidency.
The firing of General Douglas MacArthur by President Truman for insubordination was highly unpopular and shocked the American political system.

The Korean War intensified public fear of communist subversion, leading to investigations by the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) and a belief in widespread communist infiltration within American institutions.
The Korean War concluded with an armistice signed on July 27, 1953.
The armistice that ended the Korean War is not a peace treaty but a truce, and therefore the conflict remains technically ongoing.
No formal peace treaty was ever signed to end the Korean War, meaning the conflict remains officially unresolved and technically ongoing.
The fighting in the Korean War ended in a stalemate with no clear winner or loser.
The armistice restored the boundary along the 38th parallel and established the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which was set as a 2.5-mile-wide fortified buffer.
The Korean War began on June 25, 1950, when North Korea invaded South Korea across the 38th parallel, aiming to reunite the peninsula under communist rule by force.
The Korean War ended with an armistice signed on July 27, 1953, not a formal peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.
The Korean Peninsula remains divided along the 38th parallel, which has been maintained since the war and continues to serve as a boundary between North and South Korea.
The Korean War led to the creation of a demilitarized zone (DMZ) along the 38th parallel, which remains heavily fortified and actively monitored.
The United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 82 on June 25, 1950, authorizing member states to provide military assistance to South Korea in response to the North Korean invasion.
The United States led a UN coalition in the Korean War, with the majority of combat power coming from U.S. forces.
The Korean War ended with an armistice signed on July 27, 1953, by North Korea, South Korea, China, and the United Nations, but no formal peace treaty was ever ratified.
The U.S. defense strategy in January 1950 did not include Korea as part of its defensive perimeter, leaving it vulnerable to attack.
China entered the Korean War to support North Korea against United Nations forces led by the United States.
Mao Zedong argued that allowing the US to occupy all of Korea would weaken Asian communist revolutionary power and allow American influence to spread negatively across the Far East.
China's initial goal in the Korean War was not the conquest of South Korea but the preservation of North Korea as a buffer state.
President Truman rejected General MacArthur's proposals to expand the Korean War into China and to use nuclear weapons against communist forces.
General MacArthur advocated for pushing North Korean forces beyond the 38th parallel and expanding the war into China, including the use of nuclear weapons.
President Eisenhower pledged to end the Korean War in an early and honorable manner and personally visited the Korean front to assess the situation.
